cards.definition: The fixed CPU slice a round-robin scheduler gives a process before pre-empting it. Too large degenerates toward FCFS; too small spends the CPU on context switches.
cards.explanation: Rule of thumb: set it just above a typical interactive burst so most bursts finish without being switched out.

cards.definition: A process with short CPU bursts that waits on the user; responsiveness — time to first response — matters more than throughput.
Saving one process's state and loading another's; pure overhead during which no user work is done.
A trap raised when a process touches a page that is not in physical memory; the OS must load the page from disk before the instruction can complete.
cards.explanation: Disk access is orders of magnitude slower than memory, so each fault stalls the process for milliseconds.

cards.definition: The set of pages a process has referenced in its most recent window of execution; if it fits in memory the process faults rarely.
cards.explanation: Allocate at least the working set to every running process to avoid thrashing.

cards.definition: A state in which processes spend more time servicing page faults than executing because too many processes compete for too little memory; CPU utilisation collapses.
cards.explanation: The remedy is to reduce the degree of multiprogramming, not to add processes.

drills.promptText: By what mechanism does the time quantum constrain responsiveness in round-robin scheduling when the workload is dominated by interactive processes?

requiredLinks.text: A smaller quantum forces more context switches, and each switch is pure overhead in which no user work is done.
A larger quantum makes interactive processes wait longer for the CPU, which is what responsiveness measures.
The quantum should be slightly longer than a typical interactive burst so most bursts finish without being switched out.

exemplar.claim: The quantum trades overhead against waiting, and interactive workloads push it toward short but longer than a burst.
mechanisms: Shrinking the quantum multiplies context switches, each pure overhead.
Growing it makes interactive bursts queue behind long slices, raising response time.
exemplar.tradeoff: Set it just above a typical interactive burst; below that switches dominate, far above it degenerates toward FCFS.

drills.promptText: Suppose a context switch cost nothing at all. What would follow for how the time quantum should be chosen when interactive processes dominate?

requiredLinks.text: With free context switches a smaller quantum no longer wastes CPU, so the overhead argument against a short quantum disappears.
A very short quantum would then only help interactive processes, because they wait less behind other processes' slices.
The only remaining limit is the burst itself: a quantum shorter than a burst just splits the burst, so it need not go below a typical burst.

exemplar.claim: Free switches remove the cost side of the trade-off, so the quantum could shrink to the length of an interactive burst.
mechanisms: Without switch overhead a short quantum no longer wastes CPU.
Interactive processes then wait less behind other slices and respond faster.
exemplar.tradeoff: Below a typical burst the quantum only chops bursts into pieces, so that is where it stops.

drills.promptText: Under what conditions should a scheduler prefer a long time quantum over a short one, and what does each choice sacrifice for interactive processes?

requiredLinks.text: A long quantum sacrifices little to context switches because pre-emptions are rare.
A long quantum sacrifices responsiveness because interactive processes wait behind other processes' full slices.
Prefer a long quantum when bursts are long and non-interactive; prefer a short one when bursts are short and interactive.

exemplar.claim: The choice follows the burst length of the workload.
mechanisms: A long quantum keeps context switches rare, so little CPU is lost to overhead.
But interactive processes then wait behind full slices and feel sluggish.
exemplar.tradeoff: Long bursts and batch work want a long quantum; short interactive bursts want a short one, just above the burst.

drills.promptText: By what mechanism does the working set of each process determine whether adding more processes to memory leads to thrashing?

requiredLinks.text: When the working sets of the running processes together exceed physical memory, pages of a working set get evicted and reloaded, so page faults multiply.
Each page fault stalls the process on a disk access, so once faults dominate, CPU utilisation collapses.
Thrashing appears only once memory is over-committed; while every working set fits, more processes raise utilisation.

exemplar.claim: Thrashing starts at the point where the sum of working sets exceeds memory.
mechanisms: Beyond that point working-set pages are evicted and reloaded, so faults multiply.
Each fault waits on disk, so processes stall and CPU utilisation collapses.
exemplar.tradeoff: Below the point, adding processes raises utilisation; above it, every added process makes things worse.

drills.promptText: Suppose a page fault cost no more than an ordinary memory access. What would follow for thrashing and for the role of the working set?

requiredLinks.text: Thrashing would no longer collapse CPU utilisation, because a fault would no longer stall the process on disk.
The working set would lose its protective role, because evicting a working-set page would cost almost nothing.
The whole dependency runs through disk latency: the working-set rule matters only because a fault is orders of magnitude slower than memory.

exemplar.claim: Cheap faults would dissolve thrashing and make the working set almost irrelevant.
mechanisms: A fault that costs a memory access cannot stall a process, so faults could not dominate execution.
Evicting working-set pages would then cost almost nothing, so keeping the working set resident would no longer matter.
exemplar.tradeoff: Everything hangs on disk latency; the moment faults are cheap the model has nothing to protect against.

drills.promptText: When should an operating system reduce the degree of multiprogramming rather than give a faulting process more memory, and what does each remedy sacrifice?

requiredLinks.text: Reduce multiprogramming when the sum of working sets exceeds memory: suspending a process frees a whole working set at once.
Giving one process more memory lets its working set fit and stops its faults, but the pages come from other processes.
Adding processes during thrashing makes it worse, so the remedy is fewer processes, not more.

exemplar.claim: Suspend when memory is over-committed; reallocate when one process alone is short of its working set.
mechanisms: Suspending frees an entire working set, which is the only remedy once the sum exceeds memory.
Extra memory for one process stops its faults but starves others of pages.
exemplar.tradeoff: Suspension costs the suspended process its progress; reallocation costs the others theirs; adding processes makes everything worse.

response.claim: The quantum decides how long an interactive process waits, so it sets responsiveness.
mechanisms: A short quantum means constant context switches, and each switch is pure overhead where no user work happens.
A long quantum makes an interactive process sit in the queue behind everyone else's full slice before it runs.
response.tradeoff: So the quantum should be just above a typical interactive burst: most bursts finish before a switch, and waiting stays short.

response.claim: The quantum controls responsiveness.
mechanisms: A short quantum means the CPU switches constantly and each switch is overhead.
A long quantum means an interactive process sits in the queue behind everyone else's full slice.

response.claim: The quantum sets how responsive interactive processes feel.
mechanisms: A short quantum causes many context switches, but that is fine because a context switch does useful work for the user while it runs.
A long quantum makes interactive processes wait behind full slices.
response.tradeoff: Set it just above a typical burst.

response.claim: The quantum decides how long interactive processes wait, so it controls responsiveness.
mechanisms: A short quantum means the CPU switches constantly and each switch is overhead.
A long quantum means an interactive process sits in the queue behind everyone else's full slice before it runs.
response.tradeoff: Linux's CFS avoids the problem by picking the task with the least virtual runtime instead of rotating a fixed quantum.

response.text: Page tables map virtual pages to physical frames. A TLB caches recent translations so most accesses avoid walking the table, and a TLB miss costs several memory accesses.

response.tradeoff: Below a typical burst the quantum just chops the burst into pieces, so there is no reason to go shorter than a burst.

response.claim: The quantum could be much shorter.
mechanisms: Switch overhead is the only cost of a short quantum, so with free switches that cost is gone.
response.tradeoff: Still no point going below the length of a burst, since that just splits the burst.
